newsitem.title: UK: Antimony falls in minor metals, magnesium holding.
newsitem.headline: Antimony falls in minor metals, magnesium holding.

text.p: Antimony prices came under downside pressure this week in the minor industrial metals market, faced with unrelenting offers of Chinese metal and a lack of real buying interest, traders said.

Elsewhere, the magnesium market in all its myriad forms, including unloved Ukrainian, was basically steady. Molybdenum values were consolidating, albeit at strong levels, while cobalt was drifting. Business in general was slow, however.
"It has been very quiet, and there really is very little to report," one trader said.
Antimony offers were coming thick and fast from China, with several traders reporting ample tonnage available at $2,270 a tonne.
Offtake, meanwhile, is very slow as many consumers are content to bide their time, perhaps for prices to get down as low as $2,000, some said.
Earlier this week, traders in Hong Kong reported that European bids were at $2,200, with offers C and F Hong Kong at $2,300. But offers now appear to be coming in lower still.

"The Chinese keep shipping stuff out into an unreceptive market - they are just doing it for dollars...In the long-term this hurts everybody in the industry - producers and consumers," a trader here said.
Magnesium was described as "confused', with price offers ranging down to $2,400 a tonne for Chinese material (forward shipment) to as high as $3,000 for Yugoslavian origin.
But outside that range quality Western producer magnesium was fetching levels above $3,700, while there were some reports of oxidised Chinese nearer $2,000.
However, prices for the various grades do appear to be consolidating, which maybe reflected a move by China to stem the flood of cheap offers.
"The Chinese lost money in magnesium last year, and they will not want to make the same mistake this year," one said.
Molybdenum prices were holding between $13.00 and $15.00 a kilo for ferro and $5.00 to $6.00 a lb for oxide.
Current strength continues to emanate from concentrate shortages, highlighted by lower grades at Chile's Chuquicamata mine. There has also been a lack of offers from China.
"It is currently tight, but I would imagine that the Chinese will be looking to sell into a further rally," a trader said.
Cobalt trading was slow, with prices drifting back, although traders noted that longer-term fundamentals pointed to much higher prices.
Demand is expected to boom from the aerospace industry in 1997, while the boost to the supply-side is unlikley until the end of the decade.

In the short-term the market may receive a boost from talk that a Western producer has oversold and is looking to buy back its own brands and an African producer closing one of its refineries for annual maintenance.
Elsewhere, stability was noted in manganese, as prices of poorer quality started to creep up. Respectable tonnages of good quality metal have traded at levels around $1,600.
Alumino-thermic chrome values were also stable, and the good demand being seen for metal should soon feed through into higher prices, traders said.
